analysis.one_liner: Requires oil and gas drilling waste to follow federal hazardous waste disposal rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 102 House members, sat in a subcommittee and never received a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law exempts waste from oil, gas, and geothermal drilling — things like drilling fluids and the salty, chemical-laden water that comes back up a well — from federal hazardous waste rules. This bill would end that exemption and require the EPA to decide within a year which of those wastes qualify as hazardous, then regulate how they are stored, transported, and thrown away. For wastes that don't end up classified as hazardous, it would still require stricter landfill standards, including groundwater monitoring to catch contamination.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near drilling sites, landfills, or injection and disposal wells, and anyone whose drinking water sits above or downstream of them. Stronger disposal rules would reduce the chance that drilling fluids and produced water — which can carry heavy metals, salts, and chemicals — leak into groundwater. Communities near fracking operations in states like Pennsylvania would get a federal floor of protection instead of a patchwork of state rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near drilling waste sites

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the legal exemption that lets oil, gas, and geothermal drilling waste skip the hazardous waste rules every other industry must follow, and directs the EPA to formally test which drilling wastes meet hazardous waste criteria within one year [S2] [S3].

Requires federal disposal standards for wastes that are listed as hazardous, with rules for the generators, transporters, and facilities that handle them — though the EPA may adapt the requirements to the special characteristics of drilling waste as long as health and environmental protection is maintained [S2] [S3].

Even for drilling wastes not classified as hazardous, requires updated landfill criteria including groundwater monitoring to detect contamination, siting standards, corrective action, and financial assurance so that cleanup money exists if a site fails [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, who would face new costs to test, label, transport, and dispose of drilling waste through licensed hazardous waste channels — costs that are likely to be passed along in energy prices. Landfills and disposal facilities accepting drilling waste would also have to upgrade monitoring and financial assurance. Small and mid-sized operators, with less ability to absorb compliance costs, would bear this hardest.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and waste handlers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs to the oil and gas industry — testing, specialized disposal, and upgraded landfill monitoring — would partly flow to consumers through higher energy prices, and the bill gives EPA only one year to complete a technically demanding rulemaking [S2] [S3].

Regulating drilling waste as hazardous could force it into a disposal system sized for a different waste stream, and the bill allows but does not guarantee that the EPA tailors rules sensibly to the actual characteristics of drilling fluids and produced water [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — keeping drilling waste out of groundwater and drinking water — is real and falls on the communities least equipped to detect contamination themselves. The costs are borne by the industry and partly passed to energy consumers, and the one-year deadline plus flexibility for tailored rules partially answers the objection that a one-size-fits-all hazardous waste regime would be clumsy. On balance the bill is a targeted public-health protection, though its practical value depends entirely on how carefully the EPA writes the rules it mandates.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment and the Economy Subcommittee, where it sat until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 — no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on December 10, 2015, with 101 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on December 10, 2015, and to the Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy the next day [S5].
No further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers kept their hazardous waste exemption, and disposal sites accepting drilling waste avoided new monitoring and cleanup obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators kept their exemption

for.name: 101 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill within days of introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never considered or advanced the bill after its referral; no markup, hearing, or vote appears in the action history.

against.name: Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from December 11, 2015 through the end of the Congress without action.

sides.party_line_note: All 101 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans sponsored the bill; the referral committee, controlled by the House Republican majority, never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill strips the industry's decades-old exemption from federal hazardous waste rules, forcing drilling fluids and produced water into regulated, documented disposal channels. Its interest in avoiding those compliance costs runs against the communities whose groundwater the bill protects.

industries.industry: Waste disposal and landfill operators accepting drilling waste
industries.note: Facilities receiving drilling waste would face new groundwater monitoring, siting, corrective action, and financial assurance requirements. Some operators could gain business from regulated disposal, while substandard sites could be pushed out.
